article_sentences: The Supreme Court ruled that private citizens may file criminal complaints over false election affidavits.
The verdict broadens accountability while allowing magistrates to curb frivolous cases.

The Supreme Court on Friday ruled that private citizens can file criminal complaints against elected candidates for giving false information or concealing material facts in election affidavits under the Representation of the People Act, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu said the restriction under Section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure would not prevent the filing of such complaints.
The provision bars criminal courts from taking up certain offences unless the authorised public servant or court files a written complaint.

“We hold that a private complaint alleging offence committed under Section 125A, RoP Act need not pass muster of the rigours of Section 195 CrPC as held by the High Court,” the bench said, according to PTI.

“If at all a complaint is lodged to harass an elected candidate or frivolous allegations are levelled therein, the laws of the country duly equip and empower the competent magistrates to pass such order(s) as they deem fit and proper commensurate with the facts and circumstances of each case,” it added.

Section 125A of the Representation of the People Act penalises candidates who provide false information, conceal details or fail to make mandatory disclosures in their nomination papers or election affidavits.
The court delivered the judgment while disposing of an appeal filed by Rajkumar Madki against a Karnataka High Court order dated March 7, 2025.
The High Court had quashed his criminal complaint against Shailendra Beldale, an elected member of the Karnataka Legislative Assembly from the Bidar constituency.
Madki alleged that Beldale had made a false declaration about his residential address in an affidavit submitted with his nomination papers for the 2023 Assembly election.

He filed a private complaint under Section 200 of the CrPC before the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate in Bengaluru, alleging an offence punishable under Section 125A of the Representation of the People Act.

stories.headline: How Indian space tech startups are going global and attracting foreign capital
stories.title: How Indian space tech startups are going global and attracting foreign capital
stories.summary: In October, just three months after becoming the first private Indian space tech startup to launch a rocket in space, Skyroot is fielding enquiries from abroad about its launch vehicle Vikram.“Seventy to 80 percent of the demand we are seeing is global,” says Pawan Chandana, its co-founder and CEO.Most enquiries have been from the US, Europe and Southeast Asia. In October, Skyroot teamed up with Brazil’s Concert Technologies to jointly develop a 100-kg low Earth orbit launch vehicle, while also securing a deal with US-based Reflect Orbital to deploy future spacecraft across two dedicated launches.This global interest is matched by a surge in foreign capital. Not just in Skyroot.Also Read: Beyond ISRO: Meet 5 Indian Space Startups Making Global Headlines in 2026Pixxel, a Bengaluru-based startup that works on Earth imaging satellites, closed a $100 million round in September, the largest the sector has seen, led by global investment firms Temasek and Seraphim. The company was also the first Indian space tech startup to raise from a global investor when Canada’s Radical Ventures led its Series A, and in 2023, Google made its first ever investment in an Indian space tech startup by leading Pixxel’s $36 million Series B. In 2021, Agnikul Cosmos, a launch vehicle startup, raised $11 million in a Series A round led by Mayfield India, the India-focussed arm of US-based Mayfield.Indian startups are also embedding themselves into foreign markets. Digantara, a space surveillance and intelligence company, has established a manufacturing and operational footprint in Denver, Colorado, purpose-built to service US government and defence contracts. Its other such facility abroad is in Singapore.Beyond drawing foreign capital and sewing up foreign contracts, India’s space tech startups are also building unique technologies. GalaxEye became the first Indian space tech startup to secure a landmark US patent for its OptoSAR in September, a proprietary dual-sensor technology that integrates optical and radar observation. This does not exist anywhere else in the world and is getting interest from clients in West Asia.The task now is to convert this attention into commercial success, mass production, and, eventually, sustainable global market share. The upside is huge. The global space economy is put at $630 billion, according to an estimate by World Economic Forum and McKinsey & Company in 2023, and the US accounts for most of it, followed by China, Europe and Japan. India accounts for less than 2 percent, with its space tech sector estimated at $8.4 billion.Also Read: How Skyroot Aerospace Became India’s First Spacetech UnicornGlobal PlayIndia opened up its space sector to private participation long after the US and Europe did. However, this does not faze Pawan Goenka, chairman of IN-SPACe, a government agency for promoting private space tech industry. “Our companies are quite aggressive in wooing customers outside India,” he says, adding that India’s startups are winning orders from abroad and “will be very competitive in two to three years”.IN-SPACe data shows that only half of India’s top 10 space tech companies lean heavily on the home market. MistEO gets all its orders from domestic entities, Suhora and GalaxEye above 90 percent, Digantara 80 percent, and Bellatrix more than 70 percent.The other five look outward. Dhruva Space gets 90 percent of its business from abroad and HEX20 80 percent. Agnikul describes most of its orders as international and Skyroot says its book is predominantly foreign. Piersight sits in the middle, with half of its business being international.Firms selling launch vehicles and launch-linked services skew global, while those that depend on Indian government and defence customers stay anchored at home. The overseas orders are mostly for hardware and engineering services rather than data. They include satellite structures, solar panels, propulsion systems, and full satellites and design work, which suggests Indian startups are winning abroad as low-cost, space-qualified suppliers.Companies focussed on data and analytics find that orders from overseas require more than hardware exports.Pixxel, for instance, is building a physical presence in the markets where it sells. It has a subsidiary in El Segundo, California, which CEO Awais Ahmed credits with winning the Nasa and National Reconnaissance Office contracts—a $476 million Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition Programme, giving the hyperspectral imaging startup a route to supply Earth observation data to the US space agency till November 2028.A European subsidiary is “on the verge”, Ahmed says, with West Asia and Southeast Asia to follow. The European national governments, the EU and the European Space Agency have all raised their budgets, he says, creating room for unique space products such as hyperspectral imagery. Revenue, he argues, should be diversified not only between government and commercial customers but also across governments. What gets Pixxel through the door, he adds, is technology no one else offers at that resolution, “because if you are just replicating something that someone else has already done, it becomes difficult”. Pixxel is also planning to go public soon, Ahmed says.Mark Boggett, CEO of Seraphim, the global venture capital firm dedicated to space tech which led Pixxel’s record funding round in September, frames Pixxel’s model as a template for Indian startups to transition from being domestic players to competing globally. He points out how it “has built significant technology and manufacturing capabilities in India while establishing operations in the US, giving it access to customers, talent and capital in the world’s largest space market”. Boggett predicts that the next five to 10 years could be decisive, and that India’s engineering talent, government ambition and growing private funding will “create the conditions for companies to emerge that can compete globally”.Also Read: How startups are battling the odds to launch a new space tech age for IndiaThe World KnowsDigantara’s international strategy focuses on Asian markets first. It set up a wholly owned subsidiary in Singapore in 2022 and used the city state as a gateway to Asia-Pacific, finding clients in Thailand and Japan. Anirudh Sharma, CEO of Digantara, says India’s Ministry of External Affairs has helped open doors in places such as the Philippines and Mongolia, where Digantara wants to site ground sensors. Madagascar is next. “These countries are so small that no big company will look at them,” he says, “but they are good enough markets for us to start with.”It is not a bad start. Digantara has gone on to hold US government contracts for space situational awareness and missile defence, and bought a 30,000 square foot facility in Denver; the company’s facility in Bengaluru spans 50,000 square feet.“Most of the US government customers, including the Pentagon, know of us and have worked with us,” says Sharma, adding that these are multiple contracts ranging from building payloads to designing algorithms, from software to building a spacecraft.Digantara’s American subsidiary is staffed by US citizens and operates independently of its Indian parent; it is run day to day by US citizens who make operational decisions. This helps it work with US government customers and comply with rules on foreign access to sensitive technology.Also Read: Why the success of Vikram-1 matters more than the rocket itselfThat is a requirement of the work and also a limit. “We cannot have any control over the entity… it has to be an independent entity with no influence from India because we work on national security for the US government,” Sharma says.Skyroot’s Chandana says clients from Europe and Southeast Asia, in addition to the US, are creating demand across Earth observation, communications, Internet of Things (IoT), climate and weather monitoring, technology demonstrations, and other emerging small-satellite applications. “The larger opportunity for Vikram (Skyroot’s small satellite rocket) is around dedicated and responsive access to space. Many small-satellite operators today have to fly as secondary payloads on larger rockets. That can mean waiting for availability and compromising on the timing or precise orbit they require,” he explains. Echoing the need for reliable access, Reflect Orbital Co-founder and CEO Ben Nowack says, “There’s a real launch capacity shortage right now. We’re excited to work with a new launch provider, Skyroot, to help ensure access to space.”Chennai-based Agnikul’s Srinath Ravichandran describes a quieter European presence. Agnikul has signed Memorandums of Understanding (MoU) with European players. “We have announced a few of these publicly,” he says of the MoUs with Finnish company ICEYE for launching synthetic aperture radar Earth observation systems from India, and with France’s Safran in June. “Some others are still confidential.”His company plans to fly its reusable Agnibaan rocket in 2027 and has seen interest from imaging satellite operators in Europe and Australia, and from communications operators in Europe, Japan and Australia. Ravichandran describes a shift in how overseas buyers see India. “The world knows that we know what it means to build space-grade systems,” he says, a reputation he credits to Isro’s decades of work.Other companies have taken different routes.Also Read: India can aim to be the No. 1 space power: Pixxel CEODifferent OrbitsBellatrix says 85 to 90 percent of its revenue is exports, mostly to European customers. Its propulsion systems are bought by constellation operators planning multiple satellites, none of which can function without a propulsion system. Rohan Ganapathy, co-founder, CEO and CTO, says the startup is also looking east, not just geographically but also with an entirely new piece of hardware. Its push into Asia bets on a new satellite built for very low Earth orbit (VLEO), where hardly anyone has managed to stay up.It has a collaboration with South Korea’s Telepix, an imaging firm, to fly a wide-swath camera in VLEO, around 200 km above Earth. The orbit is unusual because it is where satellites normally cannot stay. At that height the atmosphere is thin but not empty, and the nitrogen particles in it create a drag that pulls a satellite down.Ganapathy explains that a satellite that would last five to seven years at 500 km above Earth would exhaust its conventional fuel supply in just four months if it is 300 km lower. But flying closer to Earth makes images sharper, with resolution improving by four to nine times over today’s optical satellites. The lower exposure to radiation means satellites can use cheaper commercial electronics instead of space-grade parts. And it avoids the crowded orbits above 500 km, which Ganapathy likens to real estate where slots are hard to get.And so, Bellatrix’s fix is to turn the problem into a fuel. At its manufacturing facility in Bengaluru, scientists and engineers have developed electric thrusters to use the thin atmosphere’s nitrogen as propellant, which in theory lets a satellite stay up as long as they want.It was this combination that drew in Telepix. The Korean company makes cameras for satellites and approached Bellatrix, after it announced its VLEO plans, to fly its camera and offer services. A launch is planned for 2027, after technology demonstrations later this year. “When we start as a business, we always focus on Europe or the US. We tend to forget the Asian side of things. But even Asia is a very big market in itself,” says Ganapathy.Confidence in EcosystemYashas Karanam, co-founder and COO at Bellatrix, says the logic is partly commercial. “The real reason we are looking into this market (Asia) is because a lot of the Western technologies have not penetrated there, so they don’t have as much US or European supplies. And that is a good opportunity for India because we have good tech these days, and the costs are significantly better,” he explains.Bellatrix is also talking to clients across Australia and West Asia for more future contracts. Other Indian startups are finding their own unique pathways abroad.Hyderabad-based Dhruva Space has expanded its footprint beyond India through high-profile European partnerships. It has partnered with French operator Kinéis for IoT space assets, teamed up with Finland’s synthetic aperture radar leader ICEYE for full-stack space solutions, and infrastructure projects and satellite programmes with Thales Alenia Space in France and Italy.In Asia-Pacific, Dhruva has a partnership with Japan’s Infostellar for ground segment services and with Australian startup Esper Satellites for cross-border payload hosting. Its most recent LEAP-2 mission, in October, featured a star tracker built by France-based Sodern (ArianeGroup) alongside an Indian payload from Satleo Labs. “That confidence is coming in into the ecosystem that the technologies being built in India and the capability to deliver space missions from India are reliable,” says Keyur Gandhi, director, Space Regulatory and Commercialisation for Dhruva Space.However, expanding into foreign markets is also a country-specific exercise with structural barriers. Sharma of Digantara says Europe is the hardest to break into. Funding there is routed through national space agencies and the European Space Agency, with contracts returned to companies in the contributing countries. To access it, a company needs to be majority-owned by a European. Defence funding from the EU and NATO has a similar 51 percent ownership requirement. Strict employment laws make it risky to build a team on a trial basis.Selling through PartnersFor GalaxEye, which makes satellites that combine optical and radar imaging, the foreign route runs through resellers. CEO Suyash Singh says most of the startup’s customers are channel partners that sell on to their own governments, not governments buying directly. The startup’s US patent for the OptoSAR technology, he says, has helped those partners. “A lot of global customers” have come forward since the grant, he says, and some who were at the “letter-of-intent stage have signed contracts”. The contracts begin paying once the satellite is in orbit.These clients, which are based in West Asia and Europe, are mainly buying OptoSAR for dual-use purpose, particularly after the war in West Asia broke out earlier this year and also, as Singh put it “because the budgets for defence are too much”. Interest among players in West Asia was already there, Singh says, but “it has accelerated quite a bit now”.The patent has also changed the questions buyers ask, he says. Foreign customers once wanted to know who was building the technology and whether the team had done it before. “Those things are now going away gradually,” Singh says. He says that foreign customers have begun to treat India as a source of original technology and not only of cheaper versions. “The [international] customers have started to believe now that the real technology innovations can really come out of India,” adds Singh.The company’s satellite, Mission Drishti, was lost about two months after launch in May. Even so, Singh says none of the resellers, including the government’s commercial arm NSIL and about 20 partners worldwide, retracted from their contracts. They told him they would restart the clock when the next satellite reaches orbit, planned for early 2028. The cost is that GalaxEye’s plan to expand into America is on hold. With its satellite not operating, Singh says, a US subsidiary is about a year and a half away, though discussions still continue.For its part, the team at GalaxEye is still trying to establish contact with its OptoSAR satellite three months after solar flares cut-off communication.When an Indian space company wins foreign orders, its suppliers share in the gain, though it arrives in stages.Vishwanathan Hariharasubramanian, co-founder and director of Valence Advanced Materials, which makes process materials used to manufacture carbon-composite parts and is a supplier to Skyroot, says his company’s growth is tied to its customers. As Skyroot builds even bigger rockets, Valence’s supply grows with them.The Real TestPixxel’s Ahmed says India’s space tech startups have found gaps rather than replicated existing technology. One is trying optical, another hyperspectral, and two or three are on radar. It is not dozens doing the same things that are already being done in the US or China.GalaxEye’s Singh says Indian companies are strikingly consistent. Delegations from France, Japan, the Netherlands, Australia and the US visiting Bengaluru’s Space Expo six years apart saw largely the same firms still working on the same problems. Bellatrix’s Rohan adds that the constraints of India’s market have made engineers creative in cutting costs.The challenges are just as consistent.Capital, especially for higher funding rounds, remains a concern, and heftier growth cheques largely come from abroad. While government customers are slower and fewer than in the US, launch capacity is uncertain, and there are critical components India cannot yet make, such as the expensive semiconductor chips.Several founders say Indian companies have not marketed themselves internationally. Bellatrix’s Karanam says there are two kinds of companies: Those which are technically serious and market-aware and those “blinded by confidence” whose fundraising outpaces their execution.In niches where Indian technology is distinctive, such as Pixxel’s hyperspectral data, GalaxEye’s fused sensor, Bellatrix’s thrusters, Digantara’s space awareness, Skyroot’s small satellite launch vehicle or Dhruva Space’s space engineering solutions, customers abroad are paying or signing up.In launch, the gap with the US and China is real, and Skyroot’s second Vikram will show whether first-flight success can be repeated. “Our immediate focus is on establishing repeatability and progressively increasing launch cadence. The opportunity is significant because globally there are still more satellites looking for dedicated launch opportunities than there is available launch capacity,” says Chandana.Beyond engineering, Boggett says, the businesses that keep attracting capital will be “those that can translate great technology into large, repeatable revenues”. Gandhi from Dhruva Space says India needs to “now look at solving the challenge for infrastructure financing through debt and grant funding for both building infrastructure on ground for space; and building infrastructure in space for ground”.Ahmed, meanwhile, has a piece of advice for Indian space tech companies looking to scale up. “One thing we can probably be doing better,” he says, “is looking international from day one.”

A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and Justice Prasanna B Varale allowed Ghosh's appeal against the Calcutta High Court's February 23, 2026 order rejecting his bail application.

The Court took note of the period of incarceration undergone by Ghosh and the progress of the trial, observing that he had been in custody for more than two years and that only seven out of 147 witnesses had been examined so far.

"In such view of the matter, considering the period of incarceration and also the stage of the trial, we are inclined to set aside the impugned order passed by the High Court and allow this appeal," the Court said.

The allegations against Ghosh relate to two aspects: financial irregularities at the college where he was the Principal, and the alleged accommodation of undeserving candidates through manipulation of merit scores.
Ghosh had approached the Supreme Court after the Special CBI Court rejected his bail applications on January 7, 2025, followed by the Calcutta High Court's dismissal of his plea on February 23, 2026.

New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to hear, on October 26, an application concerning a pregnant journalist's allegation that Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi pushed and pulled her during the Opposition INDIA bloc leaders’ march to the apex court premises over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

The application was mentioned before Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant by senior advocate Gaurav Bhatia, who sought a date for hearing the application and clarification on whether notice had been issued in the connected matters.

Responding to Bhatia’s query, the CJI-led Bench clarified that notice had already been issued in all the matters mentioned before it on Thursday and said the application would be listed on October 26.

The journalist, Richa Parashar, who works with news website Oneindia, alleged that Gandhi grabbed her hand and pulled her aggressively while she was covering the march, following which she was pushed by his security personnel and fell to the ground.
She was subsequently hospitalised.
Parashar, who is three months pregnant, alleged that the incident took place amid the commotion during the Opposition leaders’ protest on the Supreme Court premises.

The Congress has denied the allegations, describing them as politically motivated, while party leaders and supporters have circulated videos of the incident, questioning whether the visuals establish that Gandhi pushed the journalist.

The development comes a day after the Supreme Court issued notice on a separate plea seeking safeguards against political demonstrations in and around court premises in the backdrop of the October 12 protest march.
A Bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi, while issuing notice on the plea, directed the preservation of CCTV footage and other digital evidence relating to the incident.

article_sentences: The Collector had refused to recognise the community hall as a place of worship citing communal tensions between Hindu and Christian residents.

The Supreme Court on Friday (October 16) stayed the demolition of a Church of South India (CSI) church in Thippanampatti village in Tamil Nadu's Tenkasi district, in a plea challenging the High Court order finding the structure unauthorised and ordering its restoration as a community hall.
A bench of Justice Vikram Nath, Justice R Mahadevan and Justice Aparesh Singh issued notice on the plea filed by the church trust.
Senior Advocate Huzefa Ahmadi appeared for the church trust.

The case concerns a building constructed by the Tirunelveli Diocesan Trust Association, which was granted permission in 2014 to construct a community hall called the “Church of South India Community Hall”.
The association contends that the building has since been used as a church by the local Christian community, with regular prayers and religious services being conducted peacefully.
The Trust on March 4, 2024, sought recognition of the community hall as a place of worship and permission for the church tower.
However, the District Collector rejected the application on June 25, 2024, refusing permission to convert the community hall into a church and to construct the tower.
The Collector's decision was challenged by the Trust before the Madras High Court.
Before the High Court, the State argued that the original permission covered only a community hall and no approval had been obtained for a spire erected on the building.

Relying on Rule 4(3) of the Tamil Nadu Panchayats Building Rules, 1997, the State submitted that prior approval of the District Collector was mandatory for a site intended to be used for public worship or religious purposes.
The rule permits the Collector to refuse approval if the proposed use is likely to endanger public peace and order.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court today (October 16) again reiterated its concern over the absence of a pedestrian crossing at the Delhi High Court and orally warned that, if no action is taken at the next hearing, the judges will have to come and stage a dharna (protest) near it until it's done.

A bench comprising Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice KV Viswanathan said this on the lack of basic pedestrian infrastructure at the Mathura Road crossing, which witnesses heavy foot traffic from court visitors and the public.

On September 15, Senior Advocate and amicus Gaurav Agarwal informed the court that the government added a red light, but the bench suggested speed breakers and rumble strips near the Delhi High Court crossing.
Justice Pardiwala had said the matter is very important and had warned that the judges would visit to see if the needful has been done.
Subsequently, on October 5, the Court again directed that a pedestrian crossing be installed at the Delhi High Court and the National Zoological Garden on Mathura Road on a priority basis.

Today, when the matter was taken up, Additional Solicitor General Vikramjit Banerjee submitted that the issue is before a High-Level Committee set up by the Centre to examine what needs to be done at the crossing.
To this, Justice Pardiwala orally stated that the Committee may be fine, but concrete action needs to be taken, or the bench will be constrained to direct the Chief Secretary's presence.
The bench orally warned that if no action is taken by November 25, the judges will go and sit outside the Delhi High Court in tow with ASG until the issue is resolved.
Justice Pardiwala further suggested that the Committee may include the amicus in one of the meetings.
In today's hearing, two contempt petitions were also listed for non-compliance with two previous orders of the Court.

Amicus Agarwal submitted that on April 28, 2025, a bench comprising Justice Abhay S Oka and Justice Ujjal Bhuyan had stated the Union Government had notified Section 164A(scheme for interim relief to claimants) of the Motor Vehicles Act on April 1, 2022 but such an important provision is yet to be notified for more than 3 years.

stories.title: India's $100 billion China trade deficit: Are non-tariff barriers blocking Indian exports?
stories.summary: Speaking at an interaction in Bangkok, Sitharaman said China's restrictions were preventing Indian products from realising their potential in one of the world's largest markets.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: “With China, I think our trade balance is against us, and it is growing exponentially,” Sitharaman said.
She added that China “uses non-tariff barriers unhesitatingly” and that this was “the biggest hurdle in the in the trade between India and China.”
Sitharaman pointed to phytosanitary regulations, which are intended to prevent the spread of plant pests and diseases, as one of the barriers affecting Indian exporters.
She said Indian products, including generic medicines, beef and vegetables, had “immense” potential in the Chinese market but faced restrictions.
Non-tariff barriers can include licensing requirements, product standards, testing procedures and sanitary or phytosanitary measures.

While such regulations can serve legitimate health and safety objectives, differences in implementation and market-access requirements can increase compliance costs and make it harder for exporters to enter foreign markets.
For Indian businesses, improving access to China could create opportunities across pharmaceuticals and agricultural products.

However, the extent to which these barriers account for the trade deficit would need to be assessed alongside other factors, including the competitiveness of Indian products and the composition of bilateral trade.
Sitharaman said India had refrained from imposing retaliatory non-tariff restrictions or countervailing duties on Chinese goods, despite the widening imbalance.

The finance minister's remarks come as New Delhi and Beijing seek to stabilise relations following the border confrontation in 2020, which triggered prolonged diplomatic tensions and restrictions on Chinese investments and business activities.
Both countries have since taken steps to ease tensions and resume high-level engagement.
However, trade remains a contentious area, with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar also recently saying India was not “getting a level playing field in China.”

New Delhi: India is poised to become the world's fourth-largest economy in 2027, overtaking Japan in nominal GDP terms, a report has said.
The report's forecasts indicate that Japan is expected to retain the fourth position this year but India is projected to move ahead by 2027 with an economy valued at about $4.5 trillion.
The shift would push Japan down to sixth place, behind both India and the United Kingdom, it said.
The projected change comes as India continues to post robust economic growth despite an uncertain global backdrop.
Moreover, the highlighted growth forecast for India in 2026 to 7 per cent, highlighting the country's resilience amid geopolitical tensions and external economic shocks.

Earlier in October, speaking during the release of the IMF's Asia-Pacific regional economic outlook, a senior IMF official said India entered the recent surge in global energy prices from a position of strength, supported by solid growth, fiscal discipline and substantial foreign exchange reserves.
According to the IMF, these strong macroeconomic fundamentals have enabled India to navigate the impact of higher energy costs more effectively than many other economies.
Meanwhile, Japan continues to grapple with a range of structural challenges, including an ageing population, weak domestic demand and sluggish long-term growth.
The IMF has expected that Japan's economy to expand by only 0.7 per cent in 2026.
Higher energy costs and broader inflationary pressures have also weighed on the Japanese economy.
The country has witnessed sustained increases in consumer prices since 2022 with recent geopolitical developments adding to inflationary pressures through elevated fuel and energy costs.
